tip: Πότε γιορτάζεις; (póte giortázis) asks 'when's your name day?' with just a verb – Greek packs 'to have your name day' into the single word γιορτάζεις.
Τα ονομαστήρια τα γιορτάζουμε (ta onomastíria ta giortázume) – the object is stated, then echoed by τα (ta). Greek often doubles a fronted object with a small pronoun.
να χαίρεσαι (na chérese) is literally 'may you rejoice' – the classic add-on to a name day wish. να (na) + verb makes a wish with no word for 'may'.
του χρόνου (tu chrónu) is literally 'of the year' and means 'next year' – Και του χρόνου! (ke tu chrónu) wishes the happy day repeats next year.
Χριστός Ανέστη (Christós Anésti) keeps the ancient verb form Ανέστη (anésti) – today's Greek would say αναστήθηκε. The Easter greeting is frozen old Greek.
τον Απρίλιο (ton Aprílio) means 'in April' with no word for 'in' – Greek marks time with the accusative alone: έπεσε τον Απρίλιο (épese ton Aprílio) = it fell in April.
Christmas is plural in Greek: τα Χριστούγεννα (ta Christúgenna), literally 'the Christ-births' – articles and verbs around it go plural too.
